title: Chapter 10: Six Cannot Hold
blurb: One match, one point bird, and a ring that no one on the Reedbed can cut.

blocks.text: The late light lay long and gold across Hobsmere Reedbed, so low that every reed-pole threw its shadow twenty paces toward the mere, and in their crate at centre the Tenpenny birds were bickering among themselves the way they always did when they could smell water. On the counters' trestle at the reed-line the club ring box stood open. There were six copper rings in it, and I closed five.

Joan's first. CCIII 23, the copper cold from the box and her wrist warm under it. I pressed the ends together until they met and rested my thumb on the join for a moment, the way you rest a hand on a bird's back before you open your fingers. Then Mercy's, 24, and I could feel her pulse going quick and light under the band. Then Abel's, 25. He held his arm out as steady as a gatepost and watched the sky over my head while I closed it.
Then Rhys's, 26.
"Last time in these colours, Crate," he said. "Make it a good one. The Courier's sending a man with a camera."
"Is he?"
"No. But I'm going to run as if he is."
"Then I'll watch you run," I said, because it was true, and I closed his ring and kept my thumb on it longer than on the others. He let me. He did not make a joke of that.

My own I closed last, 71, one-handed against the edge of the trestle. The sixth ring lay alone in the box, stamped 27. Lucas stood behind the rope with Wilfred Cobbing, his hands in his pockets, and he did not look at it.

Across the trestle Clemency Stannard closed six. She did it without hurry, each band pressed shut between finger and thumb in one small sure movement, and between rings she looked up, not at her own players but at my hands. She had counted my rings before I finished closing them. What the Wenlode Wing had told me after the Sluice match lived in those long careful fingers: drop any shade pulled into a Hobsmere cluster, and six will never hold. I had come to the Ringing believing the cure for the Seven was in Clemency Stannard's hands. Watching her close her last ring, I understood that she would not even need to use it. With five rings of mine and one of hers, the most I could gather round a point bird was six. It would not hold.

The counters drew the ends. Dorcas Ely shook the lot between her palms and opened them, and for once it fell our way: Hobsmere to attack the north-east Roost, the mere end, with the Northing at our backs. She wrote it on the team sheet in pencil. Then Joan took the withy from my hand onto her wrist, and the counter beside Dorcas entered her as my tether.
"A win," Joan said, low, as we walked out to the reed, "and Tarrow drop a point at Gosmoor. Anything else and Hobsmere Cutters fold, and I'll be sitting in a sump till Easter. You know all that?"
"I know," I said.

The Loose came at ten to six. The boy who has my old job knelt at the crate and drew the slide, and the Tenpenny birds came out in one brown spill and went up into the gold, forty of them, their spring gloss catching purple and green each time they turned. They went straight for the mere, as they always do, and over the water they began to quarrel, pair against pair, the flock loosening and tightening like a net shaken out to dry.
Clemency raised her six at once, and within the minute the forty-first bird was there at the north-east edge, keeping its own distance as it always had.

She herded as patiently as a heron fishes. Her six shades went out along the flock's west edge at my ceiling, each nudging two or three birds and never pushing, waiting for the flock to bend south-west toward her Roost. I raised at the third minute and herded against her, edge on edge. Joan and I had chalked the day on the Dyke Arms table on Friday night: take the Breath before roost-light, and come into the Gloaming fresh.

At twenty call-minutes the counter at the north-east post called it. "Breath, Hobsmere." I dropped every shade, and for one whole minute I stood in the reed and saw only birds: forty starlings going over the water in the sinking light, the threads between them as fine as gossamer on a gate, and the one extra shape at their edge, and Clemency's patient shades at the west drawing the flock a little her way while mine were down. Nobody can settle before roost-light. I let her have the minute.

As the light went from gold to copper, the pairs began to go, two birds lifting from the edge still bickering and dropping away low toward the alders, the loft-men walking after them with their recall tins. Every pair that left took birds from the edge, where Clemency's shades were working, and more than once I saw a Fallowby shade nudge at a bird that was no longer there. My plan had never needed the edge. It needed only the core, and one bird at the front of it.
The head counter called roost-light at twenty-eight minutes and gave the counted flock: thirty-three. The doors of both Roosts stood open now, and from here to full dark any bird might go in.

The flock came lower in the Gloaming, as flocks do, and its grain showed plainly once the sun was down behind the alders. Tenpenny birds will cross water when they must, but over the flat mere they turn on each other and come apart, and all through the High Flight the Northing had been drawing them out across it, north-east, toward the mere end and our Roost. All through the High Flight I had been bringing them back round over the reed, the long dry way.

Now I picked the point bird, a cock with a ragged tail at the leading edge, and signed to Joan, and Joan signed to Mercy, and they came running in under it until we stood in a knot on the wet ground, near enough to touch. Mercy had come in off the flat mere with the dark water over her boots, and she did not look down at it once.
Rhys came last, down the west edge, at full stretch.
"And Dorne cuts inside," he panted, "the crowd on its feet, the man from the Courier weeping openly into his hat."

His marker came after him, as he had come after Rhys all evening: a fair, square young man in grey and gold who ran as though someone had told him Rhys was the whole of his job. He stopped a pace off. His shade, raised by Clemency at the same ceiling as mine, slid in among my five round the point bird.
Six.

I saw it turn. Six of its seven threads ran to shades, and for three wingbeats the cock with the ragged tail swung toward the mere and the north-east Roost and was ours. The flock did not come with it. They were over the water and quarrelling, every bird busy with its fellows, and behind the point bird the whole body of them held where it was, until the threads drew it back like a bead along a string and it was one of them again.
Across the reed Clemency Stannard looked at the knot of us and counted. I watched her do it. She counted six, and she knew what six could do, and she left her Tacker where he stood.

At the far end the dark was coming in from the south-west, and the flock's tail had begun to stream toward the Fallowby Roost, a thin bright line of birds peeling off under her patient shades, and the line was thickening. Half the counted flock in her Roost at full dark would give Fallowby a partial and the title, and leave Hobsmere nothing at all.
I want to tell the next part exactly, because it was the part I chose.

The light was going from copper to grey, and the mere had taken the colour it takes in March just before dark, a pale pewter with the whole sky laid flat on it, and the reed along its margin had lost its gold and gone the soft brown of a thrush's back and then no colour at all, and the cold was coming up off the water into the backs of my knees, and far over on the other shore, on his own side of the causeway, a man was standing by a gatepost with a chalk mark on it. I held on to all of it. I held on to the smell of the mud and the ragged tail of the point bird and the sound of Joan's breathing beside me, and in the middle of it, not with my ears, I heard one word.
One.

The forty-first bird was flying beside the Fallowby shade, nearer to me than it had ever come. I did not need Pollard's lens to know the number on its leg. I knew what he had taught us on his barn floor: a Wing passes a ring to another Wing by speaking its number to her, and the other raises it as her own until it is cut or handed back. A handover goes the other way, he had said, and when I asked who would ever speak a number to me, he had not answered.
It had said Not you to Hamish, and to Pollard Not tonight. To me it said its number.

I knew what taking it would cost. A handed ring stays with the Wing who takes it until it is cut, and this one had gone two hundred seasons without a cutting entered in the Loft's own book. If I called it, I would carry it, and I did not know where, or for how long.
"Joan," I said. "I'm going to call something."
"Then call it," she said.
I called, "One."

I said it aloud, the way I call any ring, and it came to me the way any ring does, light and certain, as if it had always been mine to raise. It did not go where I put it. I did not put it anywhere. It placed itself, at my ceiling, in the last gap round the point bird, beside the Fallowby shade, and the cock with the ragged tail had seven shades for its seven neighbours and stopped listening to anything else in the sky.
Held.
On the bank four counters watched the point bird held by seven, and I saw Dorcas Ely's pencil stop above her sheet, and stay stopped. They wrote nothing. They had sworn, all of them, to see forty.
Then I stopped fighting the Northing.

All evening I had been turning the flock back from the water. Now I let the held bird go the way the whole flock had wanted to go since the Loose: north-east, out across the flat mere, toward the last of the light and our open Roost. It was not against the grain. It was the grain. The point bird went, and it did not need its fellows to agree, because it no longer heard them; and behind it the quarrelling stopped, as if the birds had forgotten what they had been quarrelling about, and the threads ran forward from bird to bird down the whole length of the flock, the way light runs down a wet rope when you lift it out of the water.

They came after it across the mere. Thirty-three birds and a shade among them, low over the pewter water, the sound of their wings like rain beginning on reed, and every one of their reflections going with them under the surface, so that there were two flocks, one in the air and one in the mere, pouring the same way. The thin line that had been streaming toward Fallowby's end bent and came round and joined them, and none of it had gone in.

Clemency had come down the field toward the knot of us, running hard with her shade above her. Twice, as she came near, her shade came near ours, and each time the forty-first bird swung away from it, a hand's breadth and then a wing's length, as a swallow swings away from a gatepost, and came back to my cluster when she had passed. I saw her see it. In the grey light I saw her face turn up to that bird and know it. Then she looked away, at her own Roost, and lowered her voice to her Caller, and did not look at it again.
Nobody else on the Reedbed could have seen it, except Clemency, the counters, and Lucas behind the rope.

The point bird reached the mouth of the north-east Roost and went in without a check, and the flock went in after it in one long pouring line, the way water goes through a sluice when the gate is drawn, the whole bright body of it narrowing at the door and vanishing into the thatch, bird after bird, until the sky over the mere end was empty of everything but one shape above me.
The loft-men dropped the door.

Dorcas Ely and the head counter went in to count by lantern, and nobody on either side spoke until the head counter came out and read it. "Thirty-three in the north-east Roost. Thirty-three counted. Full settle to Hobsmere."
Four, nil. The match was over, with light still in the west.

Joan sat down in the wet reed. Mercy was crying into Abel's coat, and Rhys stood with both hands on his head and said, quite seriously, "Crate. Did you see that run?" I told him it was the best run he had ever made, because it was.

The counters cut the rings on the bank. They cut Fallowby's six and then our five, one by one with the snips, and dropped the bands into the box for the Loft. Dorcas Ely cut mine last. She held my wrist after the copper came away, a moment longer than she needed to, and looked up past me to where my shades had flown, where the forty-first bird was still flying, because full dark had not come yet. Then she looked at me.

Ring No. 1 cannot be cut. There is no wrist for it. It was on my line, a weight I could feel the way you feel a bird go quiet in your hand, and no snips on the Reedbed could reach it. Nobody said so. Dorcas put the snips in her pocket and went to write her sheet.

I had called thirty-six minutes, twenty-six of them drift, and the drift came on me before I was off the bank. The Tenpenny crate was already going up the causeway on Wilfred's eel-cart to meet the Loft van, and the line to it ran straight across the neck of the mere, as Hamish's had, and as mine had after Gosmoor: across the water to the Wenlode road.
Joan took my hand.

She walked me along the margin of the mere, where the reed gives way to mud and the mud to water, and she held on, and she talked. She told me every drain between Hobsmere and the sea, by name, and what was wrong with each, the silt and the back-flow and the sluices the Drainage Board ought to be ashamed of, and she swore at every one of them, and I listened, and the minutes went out of me one at a time.

In the third minute full dark came down over the mere, and I saw the forty-first bird go with it, low across the water, and then there was nothing over the mere but the first stars. The ring did not go with it. I could still feel it on my line.

Twice the pull took me to the very edge, where the water stands an inch deep over the mud, black and very still. On the night of the Gadwell match Joan had stood on this shore with her arms out and not gone in. Now she only had to keep hold, with the water at her boots and the mere going out into the dark in front of her, and she kept hold. Her hand was shaking. It did not open once.
At the twenty-sixth minute the pull went slack, and I was standing on the mud, and I was only myself.
"Done?" Joan said.
"Done," I said. "Thank you."
"Don't you thank me," she said, and her voice went. "Don't you dare."

The Dyke Arms smelled of wet wool and beer, and the wireless behind the bar had been turned up as far as it would go. At seven the announcer, in the same even voice he used for everything, read that Gosmoor Commons had beaten Tarrow Dyke at Gosmoor, and that Gosmoor Commons were champions of the Marsh Circuit for Season CCIII.

Joan put her face in her hands. Hobsmere twenty-one. Tarrow nineteen. Hobsmere Cutters would fly in the Marsh Circuit next winter, and Fallowby Wardens, who had come to the last day top of the table, would go to the playoffs instead.

Clemency Stannard came to sign the sheet at the corner table, where the counters sat with their pens. She signed under Dorcas Ely's figures in the same unhurried hand I had seen on the protest. Then she turned the sheet toward me and gave me the pen, and when I had signed she held out her hand.
"Congratulations, Sorrel Tansley," she said. "It was very well flown."

I shook it. Her hand was cool and quite steady. She did not ask me what I had seen, and I did not ask her. Then she buttoned her grey and gold coat and went out into the dark, and Rhys, who had not spoken to her since he signed, watched the door close behind her for a long time.
At the cottage Joan made tea that neither of us drank, and when I said goodnight she followed me to the back bedroom and stood in the doorway.
"Something's still on you," she said. "I felt it on the bank, after. Your hand kept turning in mine."
"Yes," I said. "They couldn't cut it. I can feel it. It isn't drift. It doesn't feel like drift."

She looked at me for a while. Then she untied the withy from her own wrist, and took mine, and bound the two together with it, knotting it the way the cutters knot a reed bundle, tight, with the tail tucked under.
"Then if you go anywhere tonight," she said, "you're taking me."

She pulled the chair to the side of the bed and sat in it in her coat, our wrists lying together on the blanket, and I lay and listened to the wind off the mere in the thatch, and some time after that I slept.

That night, with ring No. 1 still on my line, I got up in my sleep and walked north-east, out of the cottage and down the Hobsmere road toward the long levels and the sea at Saltholm, and I knew nothing of it until I woke on the causeway at two in the morning, under a sky so thick with stars that the mere held them too, the mist breathing off the black water on either side of me in slow white breaths, my bare feet on the cold stones and every part of me still walking. I was pulled up short against Joan's wrist, which she had tied to mine with the withy before I slept, and which she was holding back now with the whole of her weight, Joan who cannot swim, her boots set hard in the middle of the causeway and the dark water on both sides of her. And even awake, even with her hand locked round mine, I could feel it pulling, north-east, as steady as a tide.
